meta.blurb: Samuel Smiles asks what makes a person truly worth admiring. Through true stories of mothers, soldiers, nurses and workers, he shows that honesty, courage and self-control matter more than money, and that anyone can build a good character.
meta.bible: Samuel Smiles: Scottish writer; Character was published in 1871, after his earlier book Self-Help. Character: the book's subject, the sum of a person's habits of mind and conduct, shown in what a person does and not in what a person says. Napoleon: French emperor who is said to have believed that a child's future conduct depends on its mother. Charles Darwin: English naturalist who spent about eight years studying Barnacles. Thomas More: English statesman who refused an oath against his conscience and was executed in 1535. Birkenhead: a British troopship that sank off South Africa in 1852; the soldiers stood in ranks while the women and children left in boats. Florence Nightingale: British nurse who in 1854 went to the Crimea, to the hospital at Scutari, and made it cleaner and safer. Isaac Newton: English scientist; a well-known story says his little dog Diamond once knocked over a candle and burned his papers, and he stayed gentle. Thomas Jefferson: American president known for the advice to count ten when angry. Crimea. Scutari. England. France. Scotland. America. South Africa. Voice and tone: calm, warm and serious, practical advice illustrated by true stories; no gore; stories told as stories (say 'is said' or 'a story says') where the facts are legend.

C1C2: In 1871 Samuel Smiles, the author of Self-Help, published a second book about the quality that he valued most of all, which he simply called character. He argued that it is not a gift received at birth but something built, day by day, out of countless small decisions. The book is full of true stories that show how ordinary people have built it.

Wealth can be lost in a single bad year, and cleverness can be turned to cruel or selfish purposes, but a good character remains a power that no misfortune can take away. People trust and follow the man or woman of honest character, Smiles argues, even when they cannot explain why. Such influence is quiet, but over time it moves more people than loud speeches or large fortunes.

It is easy to talk about honesty and kindness, Smiles observes, but character is revealed only in conduct, and especially in the small, unnoticed acts of ordinary days. How we treat a stranger, a servant or a child when no one is watching tells more about us than any speech. The truest portrait of a person, he suggests, is painted not by his words but by the habits of his daily life.

The first school every child attends, Smiles says, is the home, and its lessons are the ones that go deepest and last longest. A child learns manners, speech and attitudes long before anyone teaches him to read, and these early habits often shape his whole life. The influence of the family is therefore more powerful than that of any teacher or any book.

Smiles gives special honour to mothers, whose patience and example, he says, mould the hearts of their children more than any later teaching can. Napoleon himself is said to have declared that a child's future conduct depends entirely on his mother, and many great men have said something similar about their own. Nothing in the world, Smiles adds, is more powerful than a mother's steady and unselfish love.

Children are keen observers, Smiles reminds parents, and they notice what we do far more than they remember what we tell them. A father who lectures about honesty but cheats in small things will teach his children to cheat, while one who is truthful in all his dealings teaches without ever saying a word. Example, in the home as everywhere else, speaks much louder than advice, and children are the quickest of all to hear it.

Where love, patience and good humour are the habits of the family, Smiles believes, the children grow up gentle and generous, and the household becomes a small model of how the world might be. Unkind words and sullen silences, on the other hand, are lessons too, and children learn them just as quickly. A kindly home, he concludes, is the best preparation that any child can have for the long road of life.

We are influenced, Smiles points out, by the people with whom we spend our time, and the change is so gradual that we hardly notice it. Their opinions become ours, their habits spread to us and even their ways of speaking find their way into our own conversation. For this reason he regards the choice of companions as one of the most important choices in life.

An old proverb says that a man is known by the company he keeps, and Smiles considers it far wiser than it first appears. If a person's friends are honest, hard-working and cheerful, others will assume that he is the same, and they will usually be right. If he prefers careless or dishonest friends, he will find it hard to escape their reputation, or their influence.

Smiles advises the young to seek the friendship of people who are wiser, kinder or more skilled than themselves, for such company is like a ladder that lifts us a little higher with every conversation. To be the cleverest person in every group, he warns, is a poor way to improve. We rise, he says, by walking beside those who are already some distance ahead, and by trying to keep up with them.

To see a good person at work, Smiles says, is worth more than a hundred sermons on goodness, for it shows us that such conduct is real and not merely a pleasant idea. Seeing it, we feel a quiet wish to copy it and a growing belief that we could. A good example is therefore a kind of invitation, and it speaks to everyone who sees it.

Work, according to Smiles, is the law of life, and those who try to avoid it are rarely as happy as they expect to be. Whether a person digs, writes, teaches or builds, his labour gives his days a purpose and his character a firm shape. Idleness, in contrast, may look like a reward, yet it usually leads to boredom and decay.

Honest labour, Smiles reminds us, is a friend to both body and mind, for the person who has worked well eats with appetite, sleeps soundly and enjoys his hours of leisure. The idle person, by contrast, finds that time hangs heavily and that even pleasures soon grow dull. A well-earned rest, he implies, is far sweeter than a rest that has not been earned.

Smiles urges his readers to do everything they undertake as well as they can, however small or humble the task may seem. The habit of doing a little thing well prepares us to do great things well, while careless work, once it becomes a habit, will spoil even the best opportunities. A person's work, in the end, is a portrait of the person who made it.

The English naturalist Charles Darwin devoted about eight years of his life to the careful study of barnacles, which are small sea animals that live fixed to rocks and ships. The work was slow and often tedious, yet it trained his eye and his patience for the larger questions that came later. Great achievements, the story reminds us, are seldom built on quick or glamorous labour.

Smiles distinguishes between two kinds of courage: the physical courage that faces danger and pain, and the moral courage that does what is right whatever the cost. Many people possess the first without the second, and a person who fears no enemy may still be afraid of a laugh. The moral kind, he concludes, is the rarer and often the more difficult of the two.

Smiles points to Thomas More as an example of moral courage, for the English statesman refused to swear an oath that his conscience could not accept. He knew that his refusal would cost him his position and probably his life, and in 1535 he was executed. His story reminds us that a person of principle may lose everything except his own self-respect.

When the troopship Birkenhead struck a rock off South Africa in 1852, the soldiers on board, who had little chance of escape, stood quietly in their ranks while the women and children were put into the boats. Their discipline gave the others a chance of safety, and many of the men paid for it with their lives. Smiles holds up their calm as an example of courage joined to a deep sense of duty.

Smiles notes that courage is needed not only in famous disasters but also in the quiet corners of everyday life. It takes a brave heart to admit a mistake, to confess that one does not know, or to tell the truth when a lie would be safer and more comfortable. A person who practises such small bravery, he says, will find the larger kind ready when it is needed.

Self-control, Smiles tells us, is the power to rule our own feelings and appetites rather than be ruled by them, and without it even the most gifted person is like a ship without a steersman. A person who cannot govern himself will find it hard to govern anything else, whereas a person who can do so earns the respect of everyone around him. It is, in his view, the beginning of every other virtue, and it is a power that each of us can slowly learn to build.

A well-known story, which may be more legend than fact, tells that Isaac Newton's little dog once knocked over a candle and set fire to years of his papers. Instead of shouting, the scientist is said to have spoken gently to the animal, telling it that it had no idea of the harm that it had done. Whether true or not, the tale has long been used as a picture of perfect self-control.

Smiles compares self-control to a muscle, which grows stronger with exercise and weaker with neglect. Each time we refuse a small temptation, wait before answering a provoking letter or keep a promise that has become inconvenient, we make the next refusal a little easier. In time, he says, the habit becomes so firm that it feels like second nature.

Smiles reminds us that every action repeated becomes a little easier, until it hardens into a habit and finally feels like second nature. Good habits and bad habits grow in exactly the same way, which is why the choices of today quietly decide the person of tomorrow. He therefore urges us to be very careful about what we allow ourselves to do again and again.

Duty, in Smiles's view, is the steady habit of doing what is right whether or not it is pleasant, convenient or noticed. A person who recognises it stands on solid ground, since his actions are guided by principle rather than by moods or passing fashions. He regards a firm sense of duty as the very root from which every other part of character grows.

In 1854, during the war in the Crimea, Florence Nightingale led a group of nurses to the army hospital at Scutari, where thousands of wounded and sick soldiers were suffering. By insisting on cleanliness, fresh air, decent food and careful records, she helped to make the hospital far safer, and the death rate fell. It was a victory won not by weapons but by patient, practical devotion to duty.

Not everyone is called to a battlefield or a hospital, Smiles reminds us, yet each person has a post to keep and a duty to perform. The teacher in the classroom, the clerk at his desk and the mother in her kitchen are all serving others when they do their work faithfully. A quiet life of duty, he says, may be as noble as any that history remembers.

Truthfulness, Smiles declares, is the foundation of character, since without it no other virtue can be trusted. A person who will lie when it suits him is a person whose promises, praises and apologies are all worth very little. By contrast, a speaker who is known to tell the truth carries a weight that wealth cannot buy.

A man's word, Smiles says, ought to be as good as his signature, and he should keep a promise even when it has become costly or inconvenient. Each kept promise adds a little to a person's good name, and each broken one takes away far more than it gave. Trust, once it has been earned, is the most valuable property that any person can ever own, and it is built one promise at a time.

A small lie may appear harmless, Smiles warns, but each one makes the next easier, until the habit of deceit has taken root in the character. A person who excuses small dishonesties gradually loses the ability to be honest even with himself. It is much wiser, he says, to hold firmly to the truth in the smallest things, so that the habit will be there for the greatest.

In every trade and profession, Smiles says, honest dealing brings a reward that cheating can never match, because a good name attracts customers and friends alike. A reputation takes years to build and may be lost in a day, so the wise worker guards it carefully, even when a small dishonesty would be profitable. In the long run, he assures us, honesty is also the most practical policy.

Smiles regards an ungoverned temper as one of the most damaging faults of character, since it wounds others, spoils friendships and often leads a person to say things he will bitterly regret. Anger that is allowed to rule the mind, he says, will in the end rule its owner as well, and it will do so without mercy. A person who can master his temper, on the other hand, gains a kind of quiet power that others admire and trust.

Thomas Jefferson, the American president, is known for a piece of advice that has helped many people: when angry, count to ten before you speak, and if very angry, count to a hundred. The pause, though short, allows the first rush of feeling to pass and gives reason a chance to return. It is a simple tool, but a person who uses it faithfully may avoid many regrets.

A cheerful temper, Smiles argues, is among the most valuable possessions a person can have, because it lightens his own burdens and makes the burdens of others easier to bear. It need not be a natural gift; it can be cultivated by looking for the bright side and by being thankful for small things. Such a person carries a kind of sunshine with him wherever he goes, and others are glad of it, even on the greyest days.

Manners, in Smiles's view, are the outward sign of an inward respect for other people, and they smooth the little frictions of daily life. A kind word, a patient hearing and a courteous reply cost nothing, but they are remembered long after more expensive gifts have been forgotten. Good manners are not only for the rich or the well educated, he adds, but for everyone who wishes to live well among others.

Smiles insists that real courtesy is shown equally to all, not merely to those who can reward us. The person who is rude to a servant while charming a lord reveals the shallowness of his manners and, in truth, the weakness of his character. Genuine good breeding, he says, treats the poorest person with the same respect as the richest.

Among the finest forms of courtesy, Smiles suggests, is the habit of listening, which means giving others our full attention and allowing them to finish what they have to say. The impatient speaker who is always waiting for his turn learns little and gives little pleasure. A good listener, on the other hand, is valued as a friend and often grows wiser through conversation.

Smiles holds that a character formed only in comfort is likely to be weak, for it is difficulty, discipline and honest effort that give strength and wisdom. The person who has struggled and persisted learns what no easy success could teach, including patience, humility and the true value of what he has gained. In this sense, hardship is not an enemy of character but one of its builders.

Failure, Smiles says, is the experience of every person who has attempted anything worth doing, and it is useful in proportion to what we learn from it. A sensible person examines his mistakes without excuses, takes what wisdom they offer and starts again with greater care. Many of the best characters, he observes, have been forged by loss and disappointment rather than by success.

Self-respect, Smiles argues, is a powerful guard against wrongdoing, for the person who values his own honour will refuse to do what is mean, dishonest or cruel even when no one will ever find out. It differs from vanity, which depends upon the opinion of others, because it rests on the quiet knowledge of what one is. Such a person, Smiles says, is his own best judge, and he is often the strictest one too, even when others would forgive him.

Smiles praises humility as the readiness to learn from everyone, whether they be great or small, and he warns that pride is a heavy obstacle to improvement. A person who believes that he already knows everything will never ask a question or accept a correction. The wise, he notes, are generally the first to admit how much they have left to learn.

Smiles encourages the habit of reading, which opens the mind and the heart to the best thoughts of every age. He adds a warning, however, for a poor book may do as much harm as a bad friend, and a reader should choose his books as carefully as his companions. Good reading, in his words, is a kind of conversation with the wisest people who have ever lived.

Smiles accepts that money is useful, yet he warns against making riches the single aim of life, for the person who does so often finds that his character has been spent in the pursuit. He recommends that money be earned honestly, spent wisely and shared generously, so that it serves the owner rather than ruling him. Real wealth, in his view, includes good friends, good health, useful knowledge and a clear conscience, none of which money alone can buy.

Independence, Smiles believes, is one of the finest things a person can win, for the man who earns his own living and pays his own debts is free to speak and act as his conscience directs. He is not obliged to flatter those who feed him, nor to fear those who might withdraw their favour. Such freedom, he says, is the reward of honest labour and sensible thrift, and it is worth more than any amount of borrowed comfort.

Envy, in Smiles's view, is a corrosive passion that does little harm to its object but a great deal to the person who feels it. The envious man sees his neighbour's success as his own failure and so is never at peace, while the generous man rejoices at the good fortune of others and learns from it. It is better, he says, to admire what is good in other people than to resent it, since admiration helps us grow and resentment does not.

Ambition is not evil in itself, Smiles allows, provided it aims at being useful rather than merely at being admired or at standing above others. The best ambition is to become as capable and as honest as one can, and to put these gifts to work for the good of those nearby. A person whose goal is service will often be surprised to find that success follows.

A useful life, Smiles says, is the best life, and usefulness is measured not by the size of the service but by the willingness to give it. A kind word to the lonely, a helping hand for a neighbour or a patient lesson for a child all add something to the common good. Those who live for others, he adds, tend to find a deeper happiness than those who live only for themselves.

Bodily strength fades with the years, Smiles observes, but a well-formed character remains and may even grow more beautiful with age. A person who has lived honestly, worked faithfully and treated others kindly can look back on his life with peace, and he is usually surrounded by respect and affection. The habits of a whole lifetime, he says, become the comfort of its evening, as a well-tended garden gives pleasure in the autumn.

Reputation and character are not the same, Smiles reminds us, since the first is only the opinion that others hold of us, while the second is what we truly are. A fine reputation may be built on appearances and lost in a moment, but a sound character endures whatever others say. In the long run, he insists, one is wise to care more for the second than for the first.

Fortunes are spent and monuments crumble, but a good name, Smiles tells us, is remembered and passed on from parent to child, sometimes for generations. It is the finest inheritance that anyone can leave, and it costs nothing to give except a lifetime of honest conduct. When we are gone, he adds, people will recall not what we owned but what we were.

In the end, Smiles tells his readers that character is not given but built, one small choice and one good habit at a time, and that the best moment to begin is always today. Choose honesty over ease, patience over anger, kindness over pride and duty over comfort, and these choices will slowly build the person you wish to be. Every one of us, he promises, has the power to begin, and the beginning is far closer to us than we imagine.
